name: Infections Due to Campylobacter and Related Organisms

clinicalPearls: Campylobacters are motile, non-spore-forming, curved (vibrio-like) gram-negative rods that are microaerophilic, and the genus was split off from Vibrio in 1973; over 20 species now span the genera Campylobacter, Arcobacter, and Helicobacter (Harrison 22e p.1304).

C. jejuni is the dominant diarrheal pathogen, accounting for roughly 80-90% of recognized illness in this group, while C. fetus is the principal cause of extraintestinal/systemic disease (Harrison 22e p.1304).

Undercooked poultry is the leading source in developed countries (30-70% of cases); other routes include unpasteurized milk, untreated water, infected pets, contaminated seafood, foreign travel, and oral-anal sexual contact (Harrison 22e p.1304).
Enteritis typically begins 2-4 days after exposure (range 1-7 days) and is often preceded 12-48 h by a prodrome of fever, headache, myalgia, and malaise (Harrison 22e p.1304-1305).

Visibly bloody stool occurs in about 10% of adult cases; most patients presenting for care have 10 or more bowel movements on the worst day, and cramping abdominal pain may be the most prominent feature (Harrison 22e p.1305).

C. jejuni can produce pseudoappendicitis, and isolated fever can be the only early sign, mimicking the onset of typhoid fever; myocarditis and pericarditis have been seen, especially in young men, and febrile young children may have convulsions (Harrison 22e p.1305).

C. fetus has a tropism for vascular sites, causing endocarditis, mycotic aneurysm, and septic thrombophlebitis; its protective S-layer resists complement-mediated killing and opsonization, enabling bacteremia and antigenic variation (Harrison 22e p.1305).
About 90% of bacteremic cases are due to C. jejuni and C. fetus in roughly equal numbers, despite C. jejuni being far more common overall (Harrison 22e p.1305).

The two major postinfectious sequelae are reactive arthritis (up to 2.5% of cases, no HLA-B27 association, averaging about 3.2 joints, knees most often) and Guillain-Barre syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1305).

Sialylated lipopolysaccharide on certain C. jejuni strains drives molecular mimicry against axonal cell-surface molecules; Campylobacter is estimated to trigger 20-40% of all Guillain-Barre cases despite occurring in only ~1 per 1000-2000 infections (Harrison 22e p.1305).

Diagnosis rests on culture on Campylobacter-selective fastidious media (the gold standard), with species-specific real-time PCR being more sensitive; MALDI-TOF identifies species, and Gram/Wright fecal smears or dark-field microscopy may reveal vibrioid forms with characteristic darting motility (Harrison 22e p.1305-1306).

Infection with C. jejuni in low- and middle-income countries, even when asymptomatic, is associated with childhood stunting (short stature) and a distinctive microbiome signature (Harrison 22e p.1304).
harrison.pathophysiology: Campylobacters survive in the gastrointestinal mucous layer of food animals and pets and reach humans mainly via undercooked/contaminated food or animal contact. In C. jejuni enteritis the jejunum, ileum, and colon are injured; biopsy shows a nonspecific acute inflammatory reaction with neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils in the lamina propria plus epithelial damage, mucus loss, glandular degeneration, and crypt abscesses. Strain motility and adherence favor disease, whereas classic entero- and cytotoxins (including cytolethal distending toxin) seem not to drive tissue injury; tissue invasion and occasional bacteremia indicate clinically significant invasion. C. fetus pathogenesis is better defined: nearly all clinical isolates bear a proteinaceous S-layer capsule-like structure conferring resistance to complement and opsonization, allowing bacteremia and seeding of extraintestinal sites, while antigenic switching of S-layer proteins contributes to chronicity and recurrence in compromised hosts. Protective immunity is incompletely understood but appears antibody-dependent and may be short-lived without continuous exposure (Harrison 22e p.1304-1305).
additionalDifferentials: Typhoid fever (when fever is the sole early manifestation)
additionalInvestigations: Stool culture on Campylobacter-specific selective media (diagnostic gold standard)
Species-specific real-time PCR (more sensitive than culture)
Culture-independent diagnostic tests / antigen detection (may detect nonviable organisms and give false positives)
MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for species identification
Gram or Wright stain of fecal smear for vibrioid morphology; phase-contrast or dark-field microscopy for darting motility
Blood cultures (note: low metabolic activity can make Campylobacter bacteremia hard to detect)
redFlags: Symptoms persisting beyond one week or worsening
Signs of sepsis, meningitis, or endovascular infection (suggesting C. fetus)
Septic abortion or infection during pregnancy (often leads to fetal death)
Immunocompromise, diabetes, liver disease, or extremes of age (risk of severe/recurrent extraintestinal disease)
Neurologic symptoms suggesting Guillain-Barre syndrome or its Miller Fisher variant following infection
harrison.prognosis: Almost all patients recover fully from Campylobacter enteritis, spontaneously or with therapy; the rare deaths are linked largely to volume depletion. Symptoms persist beyond one week in 10-20% of patients seeking care, and clinical relapses occur in 5-10% of untreated patients. Some patients develop reactive arthritis or Guillain-Barre syndrome. Systemic C. fetus infection is far more often fatal than infection with related species, with overall reported bacteremia mortality around 12%; outcome depends on how promptly appropriate therapy begins. Otherwise healthy hosts usually survive C. fetus infection without sequelae, whereas compromised hosts often suffer recurrent and/or life-threatening disease (Harrison 22e p.1306).
pitfalls: Labeling inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn's) before excluding Campylobacter and related infections, since presentations and biopsy findings can overlap and Campylobacter enteritis is far more common in young adults (Harrison 22e p.1306).
Assuming a negative stool culture excludes Campylobacter, as these fastidious organisms are missed without selective media or techniques (Harrison 22e p.1306).

Over-interpreting culture-independent test positivity, which may reflect nonviable bacteria and can be falsely positive, unlike culture which usually implies active or recent infection (Harrison 22e p.1306).
Treating commensal oral organisms (C. sputorum, C. concisus) as pathogens, since they rarely have pathogenic significance (Harrison 22e p.1306).
Missing C. fetus bacteremia because of its low metabolic activity in standard blood culture media (Harrison 22e p.1306).

Overlooking that not every patient with enteritis benefits from antimicrobials, and that antimotility agents can prolong symptoms and have been associated with toxic megacolon and death (Harrison 22e p.1306).
harrison.severityClassification: Three patterns of extraintestinal infection are described: (1) transient bacteremia in a normal host with enteritis, which is benign and needs no specific treatment; (2) sustained bacteremia or focal infection in a normal host, arising from enteritis and responding well to antimicrobials; and (3) sustained bacteremia or focal infection in a compromised host, in which enteritis may not be apparent and prompt, possibly prolonged, therapy is required (Harrison 22e p.1305).
management: Provide oral or intravenous rehydration and electrolyte replacement as the mainstay, since most enteritis is self-limiting and deaths relate to volume depletion
Reserve antimicrobial therapy for severe, prolonged, bloody or systemic disease and for immunocompromised or pregnant patients, using a macrolide such as azithromycin as the preferred agent
Avoid empirical fluoroquinolones because of widespread Campylobacter resistance, guiding choice by susceptibility testing
Treat C. foetus systemic or extraintestinal infection and bacteraemia with parenteral therapy such as an aminoglycoside or a carbapenem
Avoid antimotility agents in inflammatory bloody diarrhoea
Monitor for and manage post-infectious complications including Guillain-Barre syndrome and reactive arthritis
Reinforce food-hygiene and prevention measures such as thorough cooking of poultry and avoidance of unpasteurised milk
